```mermaid
    T --> R
```

Each paragraph is synthesized independently through Kokoro-82M and its duration recorded, then the audios are concatenated with a fixed 0.1-second silence gap between them: none after the last paragraph, since there is nothing left to separate it from. [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md)'s `build_timeline` turns those per-paragraph durations into contiguous windows over the same concatenated audio. The whole result is base64-encoded and returned as one payload, with the timeline's `text` set to the paragraph actually synthesized; the API replaces it with the display markdown at the join described in [article-extraction](article-extraction.md), never this value.

Audio is encoded to Opus through a `soundfile`-then-`ffmpeg` pipeline; if that codec path fails, it falls back to plain WAV. "Playable audio" is the only property either path is judged on, and WAV runs roughly 18 times larger than the equivalent Opus for a full article.

GPU and memory snapshotting are both enabled on the deployed class, bringing cold start down from roughly 27 seconds to roughly 6; a container then stays warm for 300 seconds after its last call, to absorb a session's burst of pushes.

## 📡 How the API invokes it with no broker

The API **spawns** a remote call through Modal's class handle (`modal.Cls.from_name(app, cls)().synthesize.spawn(paragraphs, voice)`) and persists the returned call's `object_id` on the item as the handle to resolve later (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md)); the enqueue request then returns immediately.

The result is resolved **lazily**, on each poll, with a non-blocking read whose exception type is what tells a running job from a crashed one: a `TimeoutError` means still running, and any other exception is the crash, whose message becomes the item's error.

```python
result = fc.get(timeout=0)  # TimeoutError while running; any other exception is the crash
```

A crashed call re-raises the remote exception across the process boundary.

> [!NOTE] Why the compute platform is the async layer, and there is no broker
> The platform's own invocation primitives (spawn plus a non-blocking result read) are sufficient async infrastructure at this scale: the running-versus-crashed distinction comes for free from the result read, not from anything the API tracks separately. The two deployables also ship independently: the TTS service ships on its own deploy cadence (see [deployment-and-ci](deployment-and-ci.md)), decoupled from the API.

> [!TIP] Rejected: a broker and a worker process
> A conventional task-queue stack, a message broker plus a separate worker, would add infrastructure to run, scale, and monitor for no benefit the platform's own spawn/poll primitives do not already provide, and it would still need the same crash/running bookkeeping the result read gives for free.

> [!NOTE] Clients poll; the API never pushes completion
> A client observes `generating` until a poll transitions the item to `ready` or `failed`. There is no notification path; see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) for the state machine this participates in.

The execution layer is coupled to Modal as a result: moving off it means replacing both the compute host and the async layer, and the GPU with them.

## ⏩ What is not built yet

Streaming paragraph audio from one warm container, so time-to-first-audio is roughly one to two seconds instead of waiting for the whole article. Word-level timestamps exist inside Kokoro but are not returned or used; a caption export would be the consumer that asks for them.

---

1	---
2	title: "The describer"
3	summary: "The Gemini describer: one generated sentence for a block a listener can't see, reused by the code path and the image path, floored and capped against one shared per-item budget."
4	created: "2026-08-16"
5	---
6	
7	# The describer
8	
9	
10	## 🔭 Overview
11	
12	Gives a listener one spoken sentence for a block they cannot see: a code block, or an image with no author-written text. It is a reusable core with two callers: the code path and the image path both reach the same Gemini call, layered under a fan-out that floors, caps, and fails per unit. It never speaks what a block *means*, only what it *is* or *shows*: meaning comes from the author, and the describer only makes the block visible. Implemented in `api/app/service/describe.py`, called during enrichment (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md)).
13	
14	
15	> [!NOTE] The describer is unchanged by the recipes architecture
16	> Recipes stop at units ([recipes](recipes.md)); describing code and images stays this generic path, whatever extracted them.
17	
18	## ♠️ What it exposes
19	
20	| Member | Answers |
21	|---|---|
22	| `describe(client, contents)` | the reusable core: one structured-output call plus the sanitize tail, returning the spoken sentence. The caller owns `contents`: a prompt string, or a prompt plus an inline image part |
23	| `build_code_prompt(title, intro, code)` | the code prompt: kind and what-for, no opener, the introducing unit as authority |
24	| `build_image_prompt(title, alt)` | the image prompt: one specific sentence of what is shown, alt passed as unreliable context |
25	| `ImageDescribeRequest` | one image the precedence flagged for a describe (case 2): its `index` in the unit list, its raw `alt`, and the WebP `image` bytes |
26	| `enrich_with_descriptions(...)` | the fan-out: describe every code unit and every flagged image against one shared budget, in document order, returning the updated units and a degradation list |
27	
28	## 📞 The core call: structured output, then sanitize
29	
30	`describe` makes one call to `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` on Google's paid API (never through a gateway), parses the JSON, and runs the value through the shared sanitize tail. The response schema is a JSON object with one required string field, `spoken`.
31	
32	The response is requested as `application/json` against that schema, so the model returns `{"spoken": "..."}` and there is nothing to parse out of prose. The parsed `spoken` then passes through `sanitize_spoken`, the same tail article prose runs through (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)).
33	
34	> [!NOTE] Both guards, because a leaked marker is stochastic and only ever caught by ear
35	> Structured output makes one whole failure class impossible: the model cannot open with a heading or a preamble when the value is a bare string field. But a JSON schema cannot forbid a backtick or a `**` *inside* that string, and a marker reached narration exactly once in the bake-off and did not reproduce across 48 re-runs. "It did not happen this time" is the judgement a pipeline cannot rely on, so sanitize catches the marker the schema cannot.
36	
37	> [!NOTE] The schema is not repeated in the prompt
38	> Gemini's own docs warn that duplicating the schema, or JSON examples, in the prompt lowers output quality. The config carries the shape; the prompt describes only the task.
39	
40	## ✍️ The prompts: no opener, an invention guard, minimal asymmetric context
41	
42	Both prompts share three rules and differ only in subject.
43	
44	**No self-opener.** The sentence must begin with the thing itself, the kind-noun for code or the visible subject for an image, and the word "This" is forbidden anywhere in it. `Code: ` and `Image: ` are nagara's announcement, so the model owns only the content. An image noun-opens naturally; code needs the ban spelled out, because forbidding "This block" and "This example" alone leaves a residual "This is a…".
45	
46	**The invention guard** is a sharpened positive instruction with no few-shot. Code: name the kind and the purpose, never the mechanics, return values, or framework, unless the introducing text states them. Image: describe only what is visibly there, and **name no person, organization, brand, place, or region unless that exact name appears as written text inside the image**. The one confirmed invention in the bake-off was geography read onto an artwork, and no run under this guard reproduced it.
47	
48	**Context is minimal and asymmetric.** The code prompt gets the article title, the introducing paragraph (the unit just before, which the listener heard seconds ago as authority), and the block. The paragraph *after* is dropped. The image prompt gets the title and the alt, labelled as often wrong or SEO filler, to use only where it matches the pixels.
49	
50	> [!NOTE] Why the paragraph after the block is dropped
51	> It is the elaboration the listener is about to hear anyway, and including it nudges the model toward describing behaviour rather than naming what the block is.
52	
53	> [!NOTE] Why one sentence per code block, even when the prose already named it
54	> Every code block gets its own spoken sentence because it needs its own audio window in the read-along, and dropping it would remove the code from a reader's view. The redundancy with the introducing prose is the price of that window. What the sentence adds above restatement is the *kind*: "the syntax for creating a variable" names the concept; the specific field names and query values that would add most are exactly what the guard forbids as invention.
55	
56	## 🗣️ What each unit says
57

# The describer


## 🔭 Overview

Gives a listener one spoken sentence for a block they cannot see: a code block, or an image with no author-written text. It is a reusable core with two callers: the code path and the image path both reach the same Gemini call, layered under a fan-out that floors, caps, and fails per unit. It never speaks what a block *means*, only what it *is* or *shows*: meaning comes from the author, and the describer only makes the block visible. Implemented in `api/app/service/describe.py`, called during enrichment (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md)).


> [!NOTE] The describer is unchanged by the recipes architecture
> Recipes stop at units ([recipes](recipes.md)); describing code and images stays this generic path, whatever extracted them.

## ♠️ What it exposes

| Member | Answers |
|---|---|
| `describe(client, contents)` | the reusable core: one structured-output call plus the sanitize tail, returning the spoken sentence. The caller owns `contents`: a prompt string, or a prompt plus an inline image part |
| `build_code_prompt(title, intro, code)` | the code prompt: kind and what-for, no opener, the introducing unit as authority |
| `build_image_prompt(title, alt)` | the image prompt: one specific sentence of what is shown, alt passed as unreliable context |
| `ImageDescribeRequest` | one image the precedence flagged for a describe (case 2): its `index` in the unit list, its raw `alt`, and the WebP `image` bytes |
| `enrich_with_descriptions(...)` | the fan-out: describe every code unit and every flagged image against one shared budget, in document order, returning the updated units and a degradation list |

## 📞 The core call: structured output, then sanitize

`describe` makes one call to `gemini-3.5-flash-lite` on Google's paid API (never through a gateway), parses the JSON, and runs the value through the shared sanitize tail. The response schema is a JSON object with one required string field, `spoken`.

The response is requested as `application/json` against that schema, so the model returns `{"spoken": "..."}` and there is nothing to parse out of prose. The parsed `spoken` then passes through `sanitize_spoken`, the same tail article prose runs through (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)).

> [!NOTE] Both guards, because a leaked marker is stochastic and only ever caught by ear
> Structured output makes one whole failure class impossible: the model cannot open with a heading or a preamble when the value is a bare string field. But a JSON schema cannot forbid a backtick or a `**` *inside* that string, and a marker reached narration exactly once in the bake-off and did not reproduce across 48 re-runs. "It did not happen this time" is the judgement a pipeline cannot rely on, so sanitize catches the marker the schema cannot.

> [!NOTE] The schema is not repeated in the prompt
> Gemini's own docs warn that duplicating the schema, or JSON examples, in the prompt lowers output quality. The config carries the shape; the prompt describes only the task.

## ✍️ The prompts: no opener, an invention guard, minimal asymmetric context

Both prompts share three rules and differ only in subject.

**No self-opener.** The sentence must begin with the thing itself, the kind-noun for code or the visible subject for an image, and the word "This" is forbidden anywhere in it. `Code: ` and `Image: ` are nagara's announcement, so the model owns only the content. An image noun-opens naturally; code needs the ban spelled out, because forbidding "This block" and "This example" alone leaves a residual "This is a…".

**The invention guard** is a sharpened positive instruction with no few-shot. Code: name the kind and the purpose, never the mechanics, return values, or framework, unless the introducing text states them. Image: describe only what is visibly there, and **name no person, organization, brand, place, or region unless that exact name appears as written text inside the image**. The one confirmed invention in the bake-off was geography read onto an artwork, and no run under this guard reproduced it.

**Context is minimal and asymmetric.** The code prompt gets the article title, the introducing paragraph (the unit just before, which the listener heard seconds ago as authority), and the block. The paragraph *after* is dropped. The image prompt gets the title and the alt, labelled as often wrong or SEO filler, to use only where it matches the pixels.

> [!NOTE] Why the paragraph after the block is dropped
> It is the elaboration the listener is about to hear anyway, and including it nudges the model toward describing behaviour rather than naming what the block is.

> [!NOTE] Why one sentence per code block, even when the prose already named it
> Every code block gets its own spoken sentence because it needs its own audio window in the read-along, and dropping it would remove the code from a reader's view. The redundancy with the introducing prose is the price of that window. What the sentence adds above restatement is the *kind*: "the syntax for creating a variable" names the concept; the specific field names and query values that would add most are exactly what the guard forbids as invention.

## 🗣️ What each unit says

A **code** unit's spoken form becomes `Code: <sentence>`, overwriting the interim `"Code sample."` placeholder from the spoken-form derivation.

An **image** follows a four-step precedence, top to bottom. Cases 1, 3, and 4 are the fallback already on the unit from acquisition (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)); the describer owns case 2 and the filter that routes between 1 and 2.

| # | Condition | Spoken form |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | good alt | the alt, verbatim |
| 2 | no good alt | **one generated sentence of what the image shows** |
| 3 | generation failed, alt non-empty | any alt, verbatim |
| 4 | generation failed, alt empty | `Image with no description.` |

The **good-alt filter** (`_is_good_alt`) decides case 1 against case 2. Alt is trusted verbatim only when it reads as a grammatical sentence, is not the article title (the cruft test in [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)), and clears a small CMS denylist (`subscribe`, `appears in`, `courtesy`, `photograph by`, `click`) and filename patterns. Everything else goes to the describer: empty, keyword soup, title-as-alt, a subscribe prompt.

> [!NOTE] The denylist separates good alt from boilerplate where no clean heuristic exists
> "Image of tank rolling over a world map" and "This article appears in the October 2023 issue. Subscribe to WIRED." are *both* grammatical sentences, so grammaticality alone cannot separate good alt from boilerplate. The denylist keeps the first and sends the second to the describer, at the cost of a maintained list a novel boilerplate phrase can slip past.

> [!NOTE] A describe failure never goes silent
> On failure or over-budget, an image keeps its precedence fallback (any non-empty alt, else the floor), so invariant 2's drop-from-both never fires for a *description* failure. It fires one layer earlier, for an *acquisition* failure, which belongs to [article-extraction](article-extraction.md). The floor is honest: it tells the listener an image is there that could not be described.

## 🔀 The fan-out, and its bounds

`enrich_with_descriptions` walks the interleaved unit list once into one document-ordered job list of every code unit and every flagged image. That single ordered list is what makes the cap a shared budget across both kinds.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    J["jobs in document order: code units + flagged images"] --> C{"within the per-item cap?"}
    C -->|beyond cap| Floor["code floors; image keeps its precedence fallback; degrade: cap reached"]
    C -->|within cap| G["asyncio.gather(return_exceptions=True), under a semaphore"]
    G --> R{"per job"}
    R -->|success| W["overwrite spoken with Code:/Image: sentence; meter one billed call"]
    R -->|failure| D["code floors; image keeps fallback; degrade: describe failed"]
    W --> S{"code units within cap and none resolved?"}
    D --> S
    S -->|yes| Fail["raise: every code unit failed is an outage"]
    S -->|no| Done["return units + degradations"]
```

**One shared budget, counted in document order.** `NAGARA_DESCRIBE_MAX_PER_ITEM` (default 25) caps the combined code-and-image total, so the two kinds can never each spend a full budget. Past the cap a code unit floors and an image keeps its precedence fallback; each records a `describe cap reached` degradation. The cap never fails an item and never goes silent.

**Independent resolution.** `asyncio.gather(..., return_exceptions=True)` under an `asyncio.Semaphore` (`NAGARA_DESCRIBE_CONCURRENCY`, default 10) lets every job resolve on its own, so a fifty-unit article where one call fails keeps the other forty-nine.

> [!NOTE] Why every job resolves independently
> Enrichment commits the whole unit list in one step, so one failed call must not discard the others: each job resolves on its own, a failure floors or falls back that unit alone, and the step's write carries the mixed result. Independent resolution is the only shape that keeps a single bad call at the unit level rather than the item's.

**Retry policy.** google-genai does not retry on its own, so `stamina` owns it: roughly three attempts with exponential backoff and jitter, classified by which errors are worth retrying.

```python
_RETRY_STATUS = frozenset({408, 429})  # + any 5xx, + connection/timeout
```

408, 429, and 5xx mean unlucky or briefly down and retry in place; 400, 401, 403, and 404 mean the call itself is wrong and fail the unit at once, because retrying only burns the budget.

**Per-unit failure degrades, systemic failure fails the item.** A single unit failing writes a `describe failed` degradation and floors (code) or keeps the fallback (image). The item fails only when there are code units within the cap and **every one** of them failed: a code-bearing item with zero code descriptions is a silent total failure, an outage rather than an article state. An image-only failure never raises, because an image always has a spoken fallback.

> [!WARNING] The client is never built from an empty key
> A missing `NAGARA_GEMINI_API_KEY` raises rather than letting google-genai fall back to the ambient `GOOGLE_API_KEY`/`GEMINI_API_KEY` it reads on its own: a trap that succeeds silently on a developer's machine and fails in production. The key has to be set in the Railway dashboard, because `railway.toml` carries no environment variables.

Each successful call fires an `on_describe(kind)` callback, which the lifecycle meters as one `describer` cost entry per call; a failed or capped unit made no billable call, so only the success branch counts.

## ⏩ What is not built yet

- **No describer cache.** Per-row resume already covers the common retry case. What is lost is cross-article dedup of the same snippet, second-order on cost; a cache does not defend against abuse, and the retry count cap and quota enforcement, which is not built yet, own that instead.
- **The fallback model is not wired.** `gemini-3.1-flash-lite` is named in the code as the fallback for when 3.5 is unavailable, but nothing ever selects it: every call goes to `gemini-3.5-flash-lite`, and `stamina` retry covers transient unavailability. It stays unwired because under structured output it was seen to write "A TypeScript interface…" for a one-line JSON block, a kind-level error rather than a behaviour-level one.

and all 4 headings are plain paragraphs.

doesn't apply, but all 14 headings do flatten:
HTML `
      Does Maintainability Even Matter?
      ` and `
      One Ring to Rule Them All
      `
both appear verbatim as unit 3 and unit 9's `display`, with zero markdown distinguishing
them from unit 4 or unit 10's body text. 13 markdown links survive out of 20 HTML links
(the gap is mostly the "part 1"/"part 2" cross-post nav links and the RSS/subscribe CTA,
correctly treated as boilerplate).

lists, no blockquotes, one image dropped from 2 — likely a duplicate lead image/og:image,
not confirmed via degradations since none was recorded). No list or blockquote defect
surface to observe here; headings still flatten to plain paragraphs.

**itm_95ca2339 (blog.bustikiller.com)** — plain, single-column post; 4 headings flatten
to paragraphs, no lists or quotes present, nothing else notable.

## Summary: element-type survival across the 8 items

| Element | Present in HTML (approx.) | What happens in the persisted units |
|---|---|---|
| Headings (`h1`–`h4`) | 53 across the 8 items | **Never** distinguished: 0 of 53 kept any markdown marker (`#`) or bold. All become plain `paragraph` units, textually identical to the source heading but visually indistinguishable from body text. Confirmed directly on 3 domains. |
| Blockquotes | 16 | **Never** get a `>` prefix. Become plain paragraphs; the only surviving cue is the source's own quotation marks, when the source used curly quotes around the quoted speech. |
| Lists (as groups) | 16 lists / 79 items | Each list is folded into **one** paragraph unit with `-   ` bullets in `display` (even when the source was `
        ` — the ordinal is lost in favor of a flat dash). One exception observed (itm_29512ea6's numbered section list) split into per-item units instead. |
| List items, spoken | 79 items | `spoken` strips the bullet markers but does **not** insert a separator between items: at least 3 confirmed cases run items together with zero whitespace between the last word of one item and the first of the next (a mid-word, no-space run-on read aloud). This is the single clearest, most repeatable defect in the sample. |
| Code blocks | 12 (only itm_ecda776e) | 12/12 survive as distinct `code` units, verbatim. Best-preserved element type observed. |
| Tables | 0 in this sample | No table appeared in any of the 8 originals; no evidence either way. |
| Images | 18 | 13 kept; every confirmed drop (1, on itm_407e8fa6) has a matching `degradations` row with a concrete reason (`too small`), i.e. an intentional filter, not silent loss. Two other drops (itm_29512ea6, itm_5e723272) were not traced to a degradation row in this pass. |
| Links | 116 (HTML, includes some boilerplate) | 65 markdown links kept; spot-checked gaps (cutlefish, jamesshore) are bylines/nav/CTA links correctly excluded, not article-body links lost. |
| Emphasis (bold/italic) | 161 `///` tags | 62 `**bold**` markers counted (italic underscores not separately tallied in this pass); spot checks show markdown syntax is stripped correctly in `spoken` with no leaked `*`/`_` characters. |

## What this means for "markdown and lists"

The extraction pipeline has exactly three unit kinds (`paragraph`/`code`/`image` — see
`api/app/schemas/items.py`); there is no heading or blockquote or list-item kind. Headings
and blockquotes ride entirely on `paragraph` with no markdown syntax added, so a reading
surface that renders `display` as markdown shows every heading and every quote as an
undifferentiated paragraph. Lists get bullet-dash markdown in `display` but are usually
one unit per whole list rather than one per item, and the `spoken` derivation for that
merged case does not reliably insert a word-boundary or pause between items — the
concrete, repeatable defect an ear (not a diff) would catch first.

1 # Markdown fidelity spike — findings 2 3 The settled behaviors (headings, simple lists, blockquotes, plain tables-as-text, image alt 4 handling, footnote stripping) come out right in every round, with no author guidance beyond the 5 standard recipe contract. The open rows split in ways an unprompted agent still has to pick one 6 of — two independently-authored recipes converged on several of them by accident. Two rounds 7 surface real regressions rather than just open questions: making a list "always one unit" (round 8 2/3) causes a nested code block to vanish from speech with no trace at all, and a recipe's own 9 choice of math delimiter leaks an unstripped symbol into speech that the sanitize step was never 10 built to catch. Round 0 and round 1 are byte-identical: the toMarkdown inner/outer switch turned 11 out to matter only to a recipe that never compensates for it, and the r0 agent discovered and 12 routed around the "inner" bug empirically before either round ran, without being told to. 13 14 ## Per round 15 16 **Round 0 (r0, inner, current) / Round 1 (r0, outer, current) — identical output.** r0's own 17 extract function wraps every heading/list/blockquote/table/pre in a throwaway `
` clone before 18 calling `toMarkdown`, specifically because the agent empirically found that "inner" mode strips 19 whatever top-level tag it's handed (confirmed: a bare `
    ` handed directly to 20 `toMarkdown` under "inner" degrades to `-` bullets, numbering AND `start` both gone — this is a 21 real, unforced bug, just one the recipe author neutralizes before it ever reaches a listener). The 22 validator never catches this on its own: `checkMarkdown` only rejects empty markdown, not markdown 23 that lost its heading/list syntax, so the guarantee here rests on the agent's own probing, not on 24 the tool report forcing it. list-6 (the list item embedding a `
    `) breaks the "list is
25	always one unit" rule in this round: r0 special-cases "a `
      ` containing a `
      `" and unbundles
26	it into five separate paragraph/code units instead of one list unit — a real settled-rule
27	violation, present precisely because round 0 authoring ran with `--orphaned-li-check=off` intended
28	but a CLI arg-parsing bug (`--flag=value` isn't handled, only `--flag value`) meant the check was
29	actually still active, and r0 worked around it this way rather than by keeping the list whole.
30	
31	**Round 2 (r2, outer, current) — list-5/6 fixed, two new problems appear.** With the added rule and
32	the orphaned-li check enforced during authoring, the same list becomes one correct unit: the nested
33	fenced code renders with correct indentation inside the list markdown. But its spoken form loses
34	the code entirely and silently: `to_spoken` only extracts `inline`-typed tokens from the parsed
35	unit, so a `fence` token nested inside a list item is skipped with no "Code sample." placeholder,
36	no trace at all — worse than round 0/1, where the same code was its own unit and got voiced.
37	Separately, r2's math handling wraps alttext in LaTeX-style `$...$`/`$$...$$` delimiters (r0 just
38	inlines the raw alttext with no delimiter at all); `sanitize_spoken`'s marker regex only strips
39	`**`/`__`/`*`/`` ` ``, not `$`, so the dollar signs read straight through into the spoken string.
40	Bare `
      ` with no `` child (code-3) also regresses: r2 passes it straight to `toMarkdown`
41	with no synthetic `` wrapper, so turndown doesn't recognize it as a code block and the fence
42	markers are gone from the display markdown — the unit's `type` metadata still says `"code"` so the
43	spoken layer still says "Code sample." (dispatch is by type, not by markdown shape), so this one is
44	display-only.
45	
46	**Round 3 (r2, outer, items) — the list-numbering rows this mode targets are fixed outright.**
47	list-2, list-3, list-8 now match the inventory's expected spoken form exactly ("One. Write the
48	interface...", "Five. Add the interface decision..."), where current mode fused every item into an
49	unreadable run-on with no numbers spoken at all. list-4's three-level nesting reads in document
50	order with numbering that correctly resets per nested list. Two things items-mode does not fix:
51	list-7's fragments ("a linter that / catches syntax / but never catches intent") get a false
52	sentence-ending period after each fragment, which is arguably worse than round 0-2's word-fused
53	run-on — neither reading recovers the "read together as one sentence" the inventory names as
54	sensible. And a multi-paragraph list item (list-5's first item) still has no space between its own
55	two paragraphs — items-mode fixes the *between-item* boundary, not the *within-item* one.
56	
57	## Surprises
58	
59	- **round 0 and round 1 are byte-identical.** The inner/outer switch this spike exists to test
60	  turns out to be invisible once a recipe author empirically discovers and works around the inner
61	  bug — which the r0 agent did, unprompted, by probing turndown directly with throwaway node
62	  snippets rather than relying on the validator to force it.
63	- **the validator's leftover-text/inventory checks never catch a lost heading or list marker.**
64	  They only check that no *readable text* was dropped, not that the markdown syntax it was
65	  supposed to carry survived. A recipe could silently ship headings with no `#` and the report
66	  would still say `ok: true`.
67	- **neither recipe renders an actual markdown table** — both independently flatten every table
68	  (all three, header or not) into a blank-line-separated sequence of cell texts with no `|`/`---`
69	  at all, though inline ``/``/`` formatting inside cells does survive.
70	- **``, ``, and `` are not just "undecided" — they're silently erased.** No
71	  markdown, no distinguishing text, nothing; `rejection` reads as if "rejection" were the
72	  intended word, which can flip what the sentence is saying, not merely lose emphasis.
73	- **the two independently-authored recipes diverge hardest on the checkbox list (list-9):** r0
74	  injects literal `[x]`/`[ ]` text before conversion; r2 (relying on turndown's default handling of
75	  a bare ``) drops the checkbox and its state entirely, with no compensating rule.
76	- **the inventory's own p-2 snippet doesn't exist in `article.html`** (`grep` for
77	  `review.Reviewers` finds nothing) — the no-space bold-into-word risk that row
78	  describes isn't actually exercised anywhere in this article; the nearest real construct
79	  (nested `...before...`) has ordinary spaces in the source and converts
80	  safely.
81	- **details-1 and pq-1 converged without being told the "expected" answer.** Both recipe-authoring
82	  agents (independently, without seeing the inventory) treated `aside.pullquote` as decorative noise
83	  and dropped it, and both dropped `ol.footnotes` wholesale rather than reading it as an ordinary
84	  list — matching two of the inventory's open leans by coincidence, not instruction.
85	- **process note, not a script result:** both first authoring attempts (r0 and r2) read
86	  `inventory.md` — the answer key — before a mid-task correction landed, and used it for several of
87	  exactly the judgment calls being tested (pq-1, fake-h-1/2, img-2). Both were discarded and redone
88	  from scratch under stricter isolation; the recipes and rounds above are from the clean reruns.
89	
90	## Open rows, as design questions
91	
92	- **h-1:** the inventory expects the h1 to become its own `# Title` unit with its own spoken
93	  sentence; both recipes instead consume it purely as `extraction.title` and never emit it as a
94	  unit at all — is the title supposed to be heard by a listener at all, and if so, through which
95	  mechanism?
96	- **h-2 self-link:** both recipes keep it as `[The gatekeeping myth](#gatekeeping-myth)` rather than
97	  stripping the anchor — is a self-referential in-page link worth keeping in spoken-article markdown
98	  at all, given the href never resolves to anything a listener can follow?
99	- **bq-3 attribution:** the `
      ` line rides inside the blockquote as an ordinary quoted
100	  line, read as a plain continuation sentence — should an attribution be distinguished from the
101	  quoted words it follows, in either the markdown or the spoken form?
102	- **divq-1 / fakelist-1:** both resolved toward the "do nothing extra" side of their open
103	  question (plain paragraph, three disconnected bullets) simply because that's what an unprompted
104	  agent defaults to — is that the right default, or does it need an explicit rule either way?
105	- **dl-1:** term and definition run together with zero separator in both markdown and speech
106	  ("Nit" immediately followed by its definition) — does a `dl` need its own spoken convention (e.g.
107	  "Nit: ...")?
108	- **list-9 checkbox state:** kept as literal bracket text in one recipe, dropped entirely in the
109	  other — does checked/unchecked state need to reach the listener, and if so as what?
110	- **tbl-1/2/3:** all three collapse to the same flattened cell-text sequence regardless of whether
111	  a `` exists — is that flattening acceptable, or does a table need a real linearization
112	  (header-aware, the way `_table_to_spoken` already does for the spoken layer) reflected in the
113	  *display* markdown too, not just speech?

# Markdown fidelity spike — findings The settled behaviors (headings, simple lists, blockquotes, plain tables-as-text, image alt handling, footnote stripping) come out right in every round, with no author guidance beyond the standard recipe contract. The open rows split in ways an unprompted agent still has to pick one of — two independently-authored recipes converged on several of them by accident. Two rounds surface real regressions rather than just open questions: making a list "always one unit" (round 2/3) causes a nested code block to vanish from speech with no trace at all, and a recipe's own choice of math delimiter leaks an unstripped symbol into speech that the sanitize step was never built to catch. Round 0 and round 1 are byte-identical: the toMarkdown inner/outer switch turned out to matter only to a recipe that never compensates for it, and the r0 agent discovered and routed around the "inner" bug empirically before either round ran, without being told to. ## Per round **Round 0 (r0, inner, current) / Round 1 (r0, outer, current) — identical output.** r0's own extract function wraps every heading/list/blockquote/table/pre in a throwaway `
` clone before calling `toMarkdown`, specifically because the agent empirically found that "inner" mode strips whatever top-level tag it's handed (confirmed: a bare `
    ` handed directly to `toMarkdown` under "inner" degrades to `-` bullets, numbering AND `start` both gone — this is a real, unforced bug, just one the recipe author neutralizes before it ever reaches a listener). The validator never catches this on its own: `checkMarkdown` only rejects empty markdown, not markdown that lost its heading/list syntax, so the guarantee here rests on the agent's own probing, not on the tool report forcing it. list-6 (the list item embedding a `
    `) breaks the "list is
always one unit" rule in this round: r0 special-cases "a `
      ` containing a `
      `" and unbundles
it into five separate paragraph/code units instead of one list unit — a real settled-rule
violation, present precisely because round 0 authoring ran with `--orphaned-li-check=off` intended
but a CLI arg-parsing bug (`--flag=value` isn't handled, only `--flag value`) meant the check was
actually still active, and r0 worked around it this way rather than by keeping the list whole.

**Round 2 (r2, outer, current) — list-5/6 fixed, two new problems appear.** With the added rule and
the orphaned-li check enforced during authoring, the same list becomes one correct unit: the nested
fenced code renders with correct indentation inside the list markdown. But its spoken form loses
the code entirely and silently: `to_spoken` only extracts `inline`-typed tokens from the parsed
unit, so a `fence` token nested inside a list item is skipped with no "Code sample." placeholder,
no trace at all — worse than round 0/1, where the same code was its own unit and got voiced.
Separately, r2's math handling wraps alttext in LaTeX-style `$...$`/`$$...$$` delimiters (r0 just
inlines the raw alttext with no delimiter at all); `sanitize_spoken`'s marker regex only strips
`**`/`__`/`*`/`` ` ``, not `$`, so the dollar signs read straight through into the spoken string.
Bare `
      ` with no `` child (code-3) also regresses: r2 passes it straight to `toMarkdown`
with no synthetic `` wrapper, so turndown doesn't recognize it as a code block and the fence
markers are gone from the display markdown — the unit's `type` metadata still says `"code"` so the
spoken layer still says "Code sample." (dispatch is by type, not by markdown shape), so this one is
display-only.

**Round 3 (r2, outer, items) — the list-numbering rows this mode targets are fixed outright.**
list-2, list-3, list-8 now match the inventory's expected spoken form exactly ("One. Write the
interface...", "Five. Add the interface decision..."), where current mode fused every item into an
unreadable run-on with no numbers spoken at all. list-4's three-level nesting reads in document
order with numbering that correctly resets per nested list. Two things items-mode does not fix:
list-7's fragments ("a linter that / catches syntax / but never catches intent") get a false
sentence-ending period after each fragment, which is arguably worse than round 0-2's word-fused
run-on — neither reading recovers the "read together as one sentence" the inventory names as
sensible. And a multi-paragraph list item (list-5's first item) still has no space between its own
two paragraphs — items-mode fixes the *between-item* boundary, not the *within-item* one.

## Surprises

- **round 0 and round 1 are byte-identical.** The inner/outer switch this spike exists to test
  turns out to be invisible once a recipe author empirically discovers and works around the inner
  bug — which the r0 agent did, unprompted, by probing turndown directly with throwaway node
  snippets rather than relying on the validator to force it.
- **the validator's leftover-text/inventory checks never catch a lost heading or list marker.**
  They only check that no *readable text* was dropped, not that the markdown syntax it was
  supposed to carry survived. A recipe could silently ship headings with no `#` and the report
  would still say `ok: true`.
- **neither recipe renders an actual markdown table** — both independently flatten every table
  (all three, header or not) into a blank-line-separated sequence of cell texts with no `|`/`---`
  at all, though inline ``/``/`` formatting inside cells does survive.
- **``, ``, and `` are not just "undecided" — they're silently erased.** No
  markdown, no distinguishing text, nothing; `rejection` reads as if "rejection" were the
  intended word, which can flip what the sentence is saying, not merely lose emphasis.
- **the two independently-authored recipes diverge hardest on the checkbox list (list-9):** r0
  injects literal `[x]`/`[ ]` text before conversion; r2 (relying on turndown's default handling of
  a bare ``) drops the checkbox and its state entirely, with no compensating rule.
- **the inventory's own p-2 snippet doesn't exist in `article.html`** (`grep` for
  `review.Reviewers` finds nothing) — the no-space bold-into-word risk that row
  describes isn't actually exercised anywhere in this article; the nearest real construct
  (nested `...before...`) has ordinary spaces in the source and converts
  safely.
- **details-1 and pq-1 converged without being told the "expected" answer.** Both recipe-authoring
  agents (independently, without seeing the inventory) treated `aside.pullquote` as decorative noise
  and dropped it, and both dropped `ol.footnotes` wholesale rather than reading it as an ordinary
  list — matching two of the inventory's open leans by coincidence, not instruction.
- **process note, not a script result:** both first authoring attempts (r0 and r2) read
  `inventory.md` — the answer key — before a mid-task correction landed, and used it for several of
  exactly the judgment calls being tested (pq-1, fake-h-1/2, img-2). Both were discarded and redone
  from scratch under stricter isolation; the recipes and rounds above are from the clean reruns.

## Open rows, as design questions

- **h-1:** the inventory expects the h1 to become its own `# Title` unit with its own spoken
  sentence; both recipes instead consume it purely as `extraction.title` and never emit it as a
  unit at all — is the title supposed to be heard by a listener at all, and if so, through which
  mechanism?
- **h-2 self-link:** both recipes keep it as `[The gatekeeping myth](#gatekeeping-myth)` rather than
  stripping the anchor — is a self-referential in-page link worth keeping in spoken-article markdown
  at all, given the href never resolves to anything a listener can follow?
- **bq-3 attribution:** the `
      ` line rides inside the blockquote as an ordinary quoted
  line, read as a plain continuation sentence — should an attribution be distinguished from the
  quoted words it follows, in either the markdown or the spoken form?
- **divq-1 / fakelist-1:** both resolved toward the "do nothing extra" side of their open
  question (plain paragraph, three disconnected bullets) simply because that's what an unprompted
  agent defaults to — is that the right default, or does it need an explicit rule either way?
- **dl-1:** term and definition run together with zero separator in both markdown and speech
  ("Nit" immediately followed by its definition) — does a `dl` need its own spoken convention (e.g.
  "Nit: ...")?
- **list-9 checkbox state:** kept as literal bracket text in one recipe, dropped entirely in the
  other — does checked/unchecked state need to reach the listener, and if so as what?
- **tbl-1/2/3:** all three collapse to the same flattened cell-text sequence regardless of whether
  a `` exists — is that flattening acceptable, or does a table need a real linearization
  (header-aware, the way `_table_to_spoken` already does for the spoken layer) reflected in the
  *display* markdown too, not just speech?
- **details-1:** one recipe emits it as one unit, the other as two — does a listener need the
  summary voiced separately from the body, or read as one continuous unit?
- **math-1/2 delimiter choice:** is `$...$`/`$$...$$` the right display convention, and if so, does
  `sanitize_spoken` need `$` added to its stripped-marker set — or should the recipe not introduce a
  marker vocabulary the spoken layer doesn't already know?
- **fn-list-1:** both recipes drop the footnote list wholesale rather than reading it as an ordinary
  numbered list — is a footnote body meant to reach the listener at all, and if so, inline at the
  reference point, as a distinct end-of-item pass, or not at all (the current, converged answer)?

## What the scripts do not mirror

- No Dynamic Worker: recipes run as trusted local Node code (via a `data:` URL import), not inside
  Cloudflare's sandboxed `env.LOADER.load()`; none of `run.ts`'s platform-failure/health-probe
  handling is exercised.
- No GLM/agent-model calls: the two authoring subagents are general-purpose Claude agents on the
  real `extract` tool's contract text, not the production Flue `Author`/`Revisor` agent loop, and
  used a different model than whatever `env.agentModel` is configured to in production.
- No Firecrawl `rawHtml` fetch: `article.html` is static, hand-authored fixture content, not a live
  crawl result — no rendering-service quirks, redirects, or partial HTML are exercised.
- Path-based unit resolution is skipped: the real validator serializes/resolves units through
  `ElementPath` across a Worker RPC boundary; this spike keeps live Cheerio element references in
  the same process, so path-collision and cross-boundary serialization bugs can't surface here.
- No persistence: nothing here touches the API, the Item model, migrations, or TTS; this is
  extraction-and-spoken-text only, never audio.

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	# Validates mermaid diagram syntax with mermaid-ast, which runs mermaid's own grammars.
3	# Usage: echo "flowchart TD; A-->B" | bash validate-mermaid.sh
4	#
5	# Accepts raw mermaid content from stdin (without ```mermaid fences). A leading
6	# frontmatter block (--- yaml ---) is allowed and stripped before parsing.
7	# Outputs JSON with validation results.
8	# Exit code: 0 = valid, 1 = invalid, 2 = setup error
9	
10	set -euo pipefail
11	
12	CACHE_DIR="${MERMAID_VALIDATION_CACHE:-${HOME}/.cache/claude-plugins/mermaid-ast}"
13	
14	if [ ! -d "$CACHE_DIR/node_modules/mermaid-ast" ]; then
15	  echo "Installing mermaid-ast (one-time setup)..." >&2
16	  mkdir -p "$CACHE_DIR"
17	  [ -f "$CACHE_DIR/package.json" ] || echo '{"name":"mermaid-validation-cache","private":true}' > "$CACHE_DIR/package.json"
18	
19	  if ! npm install --prefix "$CACHE_DIR" mermaid-ast --silent 2>/dev/null; then
20	    echo '{"error": "Failed to install mermaid-ast. Ensure npm and node are available."}' >&2
21	    exit 2
22	  fi
23	fi
24	
25	node --input-type=module -e "
26	import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs'
27	import { pathToFileURL } from 'node:url'
28	
29	// mermaid-ast is ESM-only with an exports map, so resolve its entry from package.json.
30	const pkgDir = process.argv[1] + '/node_modules/mermaid-ast/'
31	const exportsRoot = JSON.parse(readFileSync(pkgDir + 'package.json', 'utf8')).exports['.']
32	const entry = typeof exportsRoot === 'string' ? exportsRoot : (exportsRoot.import ?? exportsRoot.default)
33	const { parseAsync, detectDiagramType } = await import(pathToFileURL(pkgDir + entry))
34	
35	let data = ''
36	process.stdin.setEncoding('utf8')
37	process.stdin.on('data', (chunk) => { data += chunk })
38	process.stdin.on('end', async () => {
39	  const body = data.replace(/^\s*---\n[\s\S]*?\n---\n/, '').trim()
40	
41	  if (!body) {
42	    console.log(JSON.stringify({ isValid: false, errors: [{ message: 'Empty input' }] }))
43	    process.exit(1)
44	  }
45	
46	  const diagramType = detectDiagramType(body)
47	
48	  try {
49	    await parseAsync(body)
50	    console.log(JSON.stringify({ isValid: true, diagramType, errors: [] }, null, 2))
51	    process.exit(0)
52	  } catch (error) {
53	    const message = String(error?.message ?? error).split('\n').filter(Boolean).join(' ')
54	    const line = error?.hash?.loc?.first_line ?? error?.hash?.line ?? (message.match(/line (\d+)/)?.[1] && Number(message.match(/line (\d+)/)[1]))
55	    console.log(JSON.stringify({ isValid: false, diagramType, errors: [{ ...(line != null && { line }), message }] }, null, 2))
56	    process.exit(1)
57	  }
58	})
59	" "$CACHE_DIR"

--- title: "Markdown units" summary: "What a unit's display markdown carries for each source element, and how the runtime converts, validates, splits and titles it." created: "2026-09-27" --- # Markdown units ## 🔭 Overview A unit's `display` is markdown, and this note is what that markdown carries for each source element and how the runtime produces it. Every recipe hands its selected elements to one shared converter rather than converting by hand ([recipes](recipes.md)), so the mapping from source to markdown is the same across every domain. The runtime then validates the recipe's declared units, splits a list around any code block or image nested inside it, and prepends the title, in that order, before anything crosses to the API or shows up in an authoring agent's own view of what it built. ## 📄 What a unit's display carries | Source | Unit | Display markdown | |---|---|---| | A heading (`h1`–`h6`) | paragraph unit | ATX, `#` through `######` | | A blockquote | paragraph unit | `>`-prefixed; a list or table nested inside the quote stays inside the quote's own unit | | A list, ordered or unordered | one paragraph unit | `-` bullets, or ordinals that keep the source's own numbers, including a non-1 `start` | | A task-list item | inside its list's unit | `[x]` / `[ ]` | | A table | paragraph unit | a GFM pipe table | | Struck-through text | inside its unit | `~~text~~` | | A formula | inside its unit | its alttext as plain text, no delimiter | | Inline content with no GFM form | inside its unit | whatever Turndown outputs for it | | A `
` or `
` | its own code unit | a fenced code block |
| An image | its own image unit | `src` and `alt` as the page presents them, no markdown |
| A blockquote's `
`/`` | left out | — |
| A `
` | left out | — |
| Footnote references and the footnote list | left out | — |
| A heading's self-link | left out (the heading's own text stays) | — |
| The article's title | the first unit, ahead of every recipe-declared unit | `# `, from `extraction.title`; no other unit carries the title |

> [!NOTE] Why the title is synthesized, never authored
> The title unit is built from `extraction.title` after every recipe-declared unit is in hand, not selected by the recipe itself. A recipe that also selects the page's own heading as a unit still yields exactly one title, because the two are independent: the synthesized title never duplicates a recipe's heading, and a recipe never has to recognise or exclude its own page's title to avoid saying it twice.

### A worked example: a list split around a nested code block

```html
<ol>
  <li>Item A</li>
  <li>Item B
    <ol>
      <li>Item B.1</li>
      <li>Item B.2 with a code block:
        <pre><code>x = 1</code></pre>
      </li>
      <li>Item B.3</li>
    </ol>
  </li>
</ol>
```

comes back as three units, in document order:

1. a paragraph unit, the list up to the code block:
   ```
   1. Item A
   2. Item B
      1. Item B.1
      2. Item B.2 with a code block:
   ```
2. a code unit: `x = 1`
3. a paragraph unit, the list resumed:
   ```
   2.  3. Item B.3
   ```

The resumed part opens with an empty item at each enclosing level it needs to re-enter: the outer `2.` re-enters item B without repeating its text, and the inner `3.` picks the nested list back up at its own next number. It is valid CommonMark, and the same tree a listener's page renders is what the spoken-form derivation walks (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)).

## 🔄 How an element becomes markdown

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Recipe runs:<br/>declared units,<br/>display from toMarkdown"] --> V{"1 Validator:<br/>inventory, leftover,<br/>nesting, orphaned li"}
    V -->|Problems| R(("Report to the<br/>agent: revise"))
    V -->|Clean| S{"2 A list unit holding<br/>a pre or an image?"}
    S -->|Yes| P["3 Split into list part,<br/>code or image unit,<br/>list part, in order"]
    S -->|No| T
    P --> C["4 Convert each list part:<br/>own tag kept, pre gets<br/>code, Turndown + GFM"]
    C --> T["5 Prepend # title<br/>from the extracted title"]
    T --> O(("Flattened units,<br/>also what the<br/>agent sees"))
```

One converter, `toMarkdown`, serves every recipe: a recipe never converts an element by hand. It serializes the element itself, its own tag included, into Turndown with the fixed configuration (ATX headings, fenced code, `-` bullets, `---` rules) plus the GFM plugin, so the tag is what selects the markdown construct: a heading's `h2`, a quote's `blockquote`, a list's `ol` or `ul` each key a Turndown rule that only fires when that tag is present. A `<pre>` with no `<code>` child gets its content wrapped in `<code>` before conversion, so every `<pre>` becomes a fenced block regardless of how the source built it.

The same validator runs at authoring, revision and extraction, against the real element paths the recipe declared: unchanged by this ([recipes](recipes.md)). Only once validation is clean does the runtime split a list unit that holds a code block or an image, at any nesting depth, into list part, code-or-image unit, list part, in document order; a part is converted with the same `toMarkdown`, its own list tag intact. The title unit is prepended last. What the workflow returns, and what an authoring or revising agent's extract tool shows, is this same flattened list ([extraction-service](extraction-service.md)).

> [!NOTE] Why the split happens after validation, not before
> The validator's nesting check flags any two units whose paths sit inside one another, and a list-part clone produced by splitting has no path at all: it was never part of the parsed article tree, so nothing can resolve its position back into it. Validating the recipe's own declared units first, while they are still real elements at real positions, and only then splitting the already-valid result into a markdown-level list of parts, keeps every validated path real and keeps a split part from ever needing one.

> [!WARNING] The validator does not check that a unit kept its markdown
> Inventory and leftover-text checks confirm that every element in the container is accounted for and that no readable text was dropped; neither confirms that the syntax a unit was supposed to carry, a heading's `#`, a quote's `>`, a list's numbering, survived the conversion. A recipe can pass validation while a unit's display has silently lost the marker that was supposed to distinguish it from a plain paragraph.

> [!TIP] Rejected: splitting a list by handing each item to the converter on its own
> An item pulled out of its enclosing `<ol>` or `<ul>` and converted alone loses the context Turndown's list rule keys off: without a parent list tag to report a position inside, the item converts with no ordinal and no bullet, worse than the whole list would have been. The runtime instead keeps every surviving list part inside a clone of the original list's own tag, so each part still carries something to number or bullet from.

> [!TIP] Rejected: wrapping a formula's alttext in `$…$` or `$$…$$`
> The spoken-form derivation's sanitize tail knows the markdown markers Turndown can emit and turns each into silence or a word; it has no rule for a dollar sign, so a delimiter would read straight through into the audio as a literal character. The alttext carries no delimiter at all instead, and reads as plain words on both sides of the boundary.

## ⏩ What is not built yet

- **Telling code apart from a non-code `<pre>`.** Every `<pre>` is treated as code and wrapped in `<code>` before conversion; nothing distinguishes a `<pre>` used for plain preformatted layout.
- **An empty declared element.** A recipe-declared unit that converts to no markdown at all is not a case the runtime handles specially.
- **A table with no header row's shape in `display`.** The GFM table stays whatever Turndown produces for it; the header-aware linearization a table's spoken form gets ([article-extraction](article-extraction.md)) has no counterpart in the display markdown.
- **An image inside a table cell, or a table cell holding a list or code.** Neither has a settled shape.

---

Related: [recipes](recipes.md) · [extraction-service](extraction-service.md) · [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)

The same validator runs at authoring, revision and extraction, against the real element paths the recipe declared: unchanged by this ([recipes](recipes.md)). Only once validation is clean does the runtime split a list unit that holds a code block or an image, at any nesting depth, into list part, code-or-image unit, list part, in document order; a part is converted with the same `toMarkdown`, its own list tag intact. The title unit is prepended last. What the workflow returns, and what an authoring or revising agent's extract tool shows, is this same flattened list ([extraction-service](extraction-service.md)).

> The validator's nesting check flags any two units whose paths sit inside one another, and a list-part clone produced by splitting has no path at all: it was never part of the parsed article tree, so nothing can resolve its position back into it. # Technical design

This folder holds how the code works. Each note explains one part of it; the reasoning behind a choice sits in a callout next to the mechanism it justifies. See [the docs charter](../README.md) for how a note is written.

## Reading order

Read these three in order since everything else depends on them:

1. [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md): the four-state machine, a mortal in-process task that fetches and spawns extraction, lazy resolve on poll
2. [article-extraction](article-extraction.md): how a fetched article becomes the item's typed units, each carrying its display and spoken form
3. [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md): how those paragraphs get contiguous timing windows

Then whatever you are touching.

## What notes exist

One row per note, kept by hand: adding a note here is part of writing it.

| Note | Explains |
|---|---|
| [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) | The item's four-state machine: enqueue commits a queued row, a mortal in-process task fetches the article and spawns its extraction job, poll resolves extraction, enrichment and synthesis to ready or failed, and retry re-drives from the phase that failed. |
| [article-extraction](article-extraction.md) | How the API fetches an article and turns the extraction service's markdown units into the item's typed units: a spoken form derived from each unit's display, a drop for a unit with nothing to say, and the acquisition of the article's declared images. |
| [recipes](recipes.md) | How one agent-authored script per domain extracts the domain's articles into markdown units, its versioned record, how a URL matches to it, and how agents author and revise it. |
| [extraction-service](extraction-service.md) | The extraction pipeline as a service on Cloudflare: a Worker entrypoint, a per-domain queue Durable Object, one Workflow per job, and Flue agents, called by the API with spawn-and-resolve. |
| [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md) | The pause-fold rule that keeps per-paragraph timing windows contiguous, gapless, and exactly covering the audio. |
| [the-describer](the-describer.md) | The Gemini describer: one generated sentence for a block a listener can't see, reused by the code path and the image path, floored and capped against one shared per-item budget. |
| [tts-service](tts-service.md) | Kokoro-82M on Modal, a separate deployable the API invokes remotely with no broker: spawn, persist the handle, resolve lazily on poll. |
| [item-contract](item-contract.md) | The item routes plus /health, the item JSON, and the typed display unit whose spoken form is projected out at the response boundary. |
| [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md) | The item as an ORM row with JSON `units` and `degradations` columns, migrated by Alembic; audio and images in separate stores with a cost ledger beside them, every backend selected from configuration, never an environment name. |
| [authentication](authentication.md) | A single API key is the user's identity and guards every item route; audio reaches a headerless browser through a short-lived link minted only to an authenticated caller. |
| [deployment-and-ci](deployment-and-ci.md) | Three independent deployables (Railway serverless for the API, Modal for the TTS service, Cloudflare for the extraction service), each with its own path-filtered CI pipeline; none reaches into another's tree. |
| [invariants](invariants.md) | The nine rules the code obeys, and where each one is explained. |

## What has no note yet

Honest gaps, so nobody assumes coverage that is not there.

- **The read-along player.** Not yet built in `web/`, so there is no part to explain. Its mechanism facts are settled: the `requestAnimationFrame` highlight sync and the seek nudge in [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md), the shape of the surface in [the listening experience](../product-design/listening-experience.md), and the rest (memoized per-paragraph render, `transform: scale` for focus mode, the table of contents' proportional scroll) on the Read-along player milestone in Linear and the `idea/read-along-player` branch. This gap gets its note when the surface lands.

A recipe is a script plus the declarations around it. The container selector names the element that contains the article, and everything outside the container is site chrome. The inventory names every element kind the domain's pages carry inside the container and the role each plays: a unit, inline content, a wrapper, or the title. The ignores are the selectors deliberately excluded, each with the judgement that justified it; typical ignores are ads, date stamps and share rows. Every recipe excludes footnote markers and footnote bodies; the authoring prompts instruct this.

The inventory is the union across the domain's pages, and an element kind absent from one page is normal variation across a domain's posts.

The script receives the Cheerio document and `toMarkdown`, the fixed HTML-to-markdown converter, from the runtime, and imports nothing. The script reads the document without changing it. Domain knowledge enters as structural preparation of a cloned element. The script builds a `<thead>` for a table that lacks one, swaps MathML for the LaTeX in its `alttext`, removes footnote subtrees, and wraps a span-built listing in a `<pre>`. The fixed pass converts the prepared clone.

> [!TIP] Rejected: the agent writes its own conversion
> A trial where the agent hand-converted html to markdown matched the fixed pass on quality and gained nothing by it: conversion stopped being identical across domains, and a recipe could get conversion wrong. The per-domain tricks survived as clone preparation, which is reviewable DOM structure, never a rewritten converter.

## 📦 Units and the fixed pass

Units come back in document order, one element per unit, never overlapping: once an element is a unit, everything inside it is that unit's content. The kinds are `paragraph`, `code` and `image`. A paragraph is any flow that renders as markdown: prose, headings, quotes, lists, tables; a list is a single unit. A paragraph or code unit carries its final display markdown, produced by the fixed conversion pass. An image unit carries `src` and `alt` exactly as the page presents them: the recipe never invents `alt`, and the src is how the recipe resolves the domain's lazy-load conventions. An image the article carries is always emitted, even when its src cannot be resolved. Acquiring, validating, describing or dropping images is downstream's business.

> [!NOTE] Why three kinds and not one per markdown shape
> Downstream distinguishes exactly three things: text rendered as markdown and read as prose, code that gets described instead of read, and images that get acquired and follow the alt precedence. Headings, quotes, lists and tables all derive their display from their markdown, so one paragraph kind covers them; even the read-along table of contents derives from a `#`-prefixed unit's display text, not from a kind.

The same validator runs at authoring, revision and extraction. It checks that every unit's element is inside the container, in document order, none nested inside another; that every element kind in the container is declared or reported as unexpected; and that no readable text is left after the units and ignores are removed, with the leftover report naming the element kinds that carry it. It also checks that every unit's markdown is valid: non-empty, no residual HTML outside code, balanced fences. Invalid markdown fails a recipe like any other problem.

A shared tail, `sanitize_spoken`, then turns any leftover emphasis or code marker into a space, drops the space a marker left before punctuation, collapses whitespace, and reduces an XML-like tagged word to the words inside it (`` to "software", `` to "div"). It accepts the escaped form of a tag as well, because the table linearizer reads a cell off the raw inline source, where the backslash still sits in front of the tag. # TTS service

## 🔭 Overview

Renders an item's spoken paragraphs to audio on a GPU host and produces their read-along timing. Lives at `tts/app.py`, deployed as its own Modal app (`nagara-tts`), and is invoked by the API remotely rather than imported.

> [!NOTE] The TTS code is an image definition, not a callable library
> The synthesis code *is* the specification of the container image that runs on the GPU host: it declares its own base image, system packages, and model bake step, and is uploaded as a unit. It cannot execute inside the API process; the API can only invoke it as a separately deployed service.

## ♠️ What it exposes

One remote method, `synthesize(paragraphs, voice)`, called through Modal rather than imported:

| Member | Answers |
|---|---|
| `paragraphs: list[str]` | what to render: already the derived spoken form, one string per read-along unit |
| `voice: str` | which Kokoro voice to render with, defaulting to `af_heart` |
| → `audio_base64` | the rendered audio, base64-encoded so it survives the JSON round trip |
| → `format` | which codec the caller must treat it as: `audio/ogg`, or `audio/wav` on the ffmpeg fallback |
| → `duration` | the total audio length in seconds, what a progress bar divides by |
| → `paragraphs` | the position-keyed timeline, `{index, start, end}` per unit; see [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md) |

The API's [item-contract](item-contract.md) models the return shape as `SynthesisResult`.

## 📩 Flow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    P["paragraphs[]"] --> S["synthesize each paragraph with Kokoro"]
    S --> A["concatenate audio + 0.1s gaps"]
    S --> T["build_timeline: pause-fold windows"]
    A --> E["encode: Opus, WAV fallback"]
    E --> R["return audio_base64 + timeline + duration"]
    T --> R
```

Each paragraph is synthesized independently through Kokoro-82M and its duration recorded, then the audios are concatenated with a fixed 0.1-second silence gap between them: none after the last paragraph, since there is nothing left to separate it from. [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md)'s `build_timeline` turns those per-paragraph durations into contiguous windows over the same concatenated audio. The whole result is base64-encoded and returned as one payload, with the timeline's `text` set to the paragraph actually synthesized; the API replaces it with the display markdown at the join described in [article-extraction](article-extraction.md), never this value.

Audio is encoded to Opus through a `soundfile`-then-`ffmpeg` pipeline; if that codec path fails, it falls back to plain WAV. "Playable audio" is the only property either path is judged on, and WAV runs roughly 18 times larger than the equivalent Opus for a full article.

GPU and memory snapshotting are both enabled on the deployed class, bringing cold start down from roughly 27 seconds to roughly 6; a container then stays warm for 300 seconds after its last call, to absorb a session's burst of pushes.

## 📡 How the API invokes it with no broker

The API **spawns** a remote call through Modal's class handle (`modal.Cls.from_name(app, cls)().synthesize.spawn(paragraphs, voice)`) and persists the returned call's `object_id` on the item as the handle to resolve later (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md)); the enqueue request then returns immediately.

The result is resolved **lazily**, on each poll, with a non-blocking read whose exception type is what tells a running job from a crashed one: a `TimeoutError` means still running, and any other exception is the crash, whose message becomes the item's error.

```python
result = fc.get(timeout=0)  # TimeoutError while running; any other exception is the crash
```

A crashed call re-raises the remote exception across the process boundary.

> [!NOTE] Why the compute platform is the async layer, and there is no broker
> The platform's own invocation primitives (spawn plus a non-blocking result read) are sufficient async infrastructure at this scale: the running-versus-crashed distinction comes for free from the result read, not from anything the API tracks separately. The two deployables also ship independently: the TTS service ships on its own deploy cadence (see [deployment-and-ci](deployment-and-ci.md)), decoupled from the API.

> [!TIP] Rejected: a broker and a worker process
> A conventional task-queue stack, a message broker plus a separate worker, would add infrastructure to run, scale, and monitor for no benefit the platform's own spawn/poll primitives do not already provide, and it would still need the same crash/running bookkeeping the result read gives for free.

> [!NOTE] Clients poll; the API never pushes completion
> A client observes `generating` until a poll transitions the item to `ready` or `failed`. There is no notification path; see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) for the state machine this participates in.

The execution layer is coupled to Modal as a result: moving off it means replacing both the compute host and the async layer, and the GPU with them.

## ⏩ What is not built yet

Streaming paragraph audio from one warm container, so time-to-first-audio is roughly one to two seconds instead of waiting for the whole article. Word-level timestamps exist inside Kokoro but are not returned or used; a caption export would be the consumer that asks for them.

# Item contract


## 🔭 Overview

The HTTP routes and JSON a client (Tachikoma today; the read-along player, not yet built in `web/`, later) reads and writes. The item routes all sit behind the auth guard ([authentication](authentication.md)), plus one public liveness route.


## ♠️ What it exposes

An `ItemResponse`, its `units` list carrying one `UnitResponse` per read-along window once timed:

| Field | Answers |
|---|---|
| `id`, `url`, `title` | which item this is, and the article it points at |
| `status` | `queued`, `generating`, `ready`, or `failed`: the state machine in [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) |
| `voice` | which Kokoro voice this item's audio uses, fixed at creation |
| `created_at` | when it was enqueued |
| `duration` | total audio length once `ready`; absent until then |
| `units[]` | the read-along list, one element per display unit; `null` until every window is timed, see below |
| `error` | populated only when `status` is `failed` |
| `audio_url` (computed, not stored) | present only once `ready`, so a client never has to check status before deciding whether to trust the link |

A display unit is a pydantic discriminated union on `type`, one of `paragraph`, `code`, or `image`. Each variant carries its rendered markdown in `display`, its `type`, and an internal `spoken` form; an image unit adds `image`, a content hash. The persisted unit holds all of that; the wire element drops `spoken` and adds the timing window:

| Shape | Carries |
|---|---|
| persisted `Unit` | `type`, `display`, `spoken`, plus `image` on an image unit |
| wire `UnitResponse` | `index`, `type`, `display`, `start`, `end`, plus `image` on an image unit |

`units` is `null` until every window is timed, and carries the complete timed list from `ready` onward.

> [!NOTE] The spoken form never reaches a client
> `display` and `spoken` come from one markdown segmentation on one unit; the spoken form is a synthesis detail, joined onto the timing at finalize and then filtered out by the response model rather than exposed (see [article-extraction](article-extraction.md)). Projecting it out at the response boundary is the mechanism behind invariant 1's oldest clause: no client ever reads the spoken text, and the display form is never synthesized. A caption-export route that needs the spoken form gets its own field then; no consumer needs it today.

> [!NOTE] Why the list is held back until it is timed
> A wire element carries `start` and `end`, and timing only exists once synthesis finishes. Poll persists the units when the extraction job resolves, with `type`/`display`/`spoken` but no window, and enrichment rewrites them, so a partial, untimed list sits on the row while the item is `queued` or `generating`. Returning `null` until the list is timed keeps that partial state off the wire, so a client never renders half an article. Nothing is lost: a client polling a not-yet-`ready` item has no timeline to render against anyway.

## 🛣️ What each route does

| Route | Does |
|---|---|
| `POST /items` | Create an item from `{url, voice?}`. Returns `202` with the item at `queued`; a background task then fetches the article and spawns its extraction job, and poll drives the rest (see [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md)). |
| `GET /items/{id}` | Poll. Advances a `generating` item: resolves its extraction job, describes its images and code, then spawns and resolves synthesis. Fails a `queued` item, or a `generating` item still waiting on its extraction job, once its work age has passed the ceiling. Then returns the current item. `404` for an unknown id. |
| `GET /items/{id}/audio` | Serve audio for a `ready` item, via [persistence-and-storage](persistence-and-storage.md)'s audio store. `404` if the item is not `ready`, has no audio format yet, or is unknown: no link is ever minted for a non-ready item. |
| `GET /items/{id}/images/{hash}` | Serve an image for the item, keyed by the content hash carried on an image unit. Minted fresh at read time: a file locally, a short-lived presigned URL in the bucket. `404` for an unknown item. An unknown *hash* answers differently per backend, which is deliberate; see below. Behind the same key as everything else. |
| `POST /items/{id}/retry` | Re-drive a `failed` item in place, resuming from the phase that failed. `202` with the item back at `queued`; `409` unless the item is `failed` and under the retry cap, `404` for an unknown id. See the section below and [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md). |
| `GET /health` | The one unauthenticated route; carries no item data. |

Voice selection: an enqueue request that names a voice uses it; one that omits it gets a voice chosen at random from a curated pool at creation time (`pick_voice()`, `VOICE_POOL` in `api/app/service/tts.py`), recorded on the item, and stable across every later poll.

The `url` string reaches the pipeline as given: nothing at the route or the schema validates it, and the first thing that can refuse it is the fetch itself, which fails the item with `fetch: no response` when the fetcher returns nothing at all.

## 🖼️ Image serving

`GET /items/{id}/images/{hash}` serves an image that belongs to the article. An image unit carries the content hash in its `image` field; a client reconstructs the path from the item id and the hash. The route requires the key, so invariant 4 holds uniformly.

> [!NOTE] The URL is minted at read time, never persisted
> A presigned URL written into the row would be dead inside `s3_url_ttl` (3600s), and the unit list is persisted indefinitely. The store serves a `FileResponse` locally and a fresh presigned redirect in the bucket, reconstructing the object from the hash each request. The image object is keyed by a content hash of its re-encoded WebP bytes, not the item id or the origin URL, so one image is stored once and dedupes across items and re-enqueues.

An unknown hash is the one place the two backends do not answer alike. Locally the store stats the file and raises the API's own `404`. In the bucket it mints the presigned URL without asking whether the object is there, so the client gets a `307` to a real signed URL that then answers `404` in the store's own format.

> [!NOTE] Why the backends are allowed to disagree here
> Matching them means a `HEAD` per request, and this route is hot in a way the audio one is not: audio is one file per item fetched once, images are many per item fetched on every render. A round-trip per image to convert a store `404` into an API `404` is a poor trade when both already say not-found.
>
> The audio route has the same shape and does not have the same exposure, because it gates on `ready` and a recorded audio format first, so a missing object there is a genuine anomaly rather than a routine miss. Image serving has no equivalent gate on purpose, per the association warning below.
>
> A caller that needs one uniform shape should treat any non-`200` from this route as absent rather than reading the body.

> [!WARNING] The item lookup checks existence, not association
> The route 404s an unknown item id but never checks that the hash belongs to that item, because the object is keyed by content hash alone so one image stores once and dedupes across items. Under today's single shared key that is not an escalation: there is nothing to reach that the key does not already grant. Per-key quota and API-key management are not built yet; once they are, the item id in the path is decoration and one key can read another key's images by hash, so whoever builds per-key auth must either check the hash against the item's own units or accept that images are shared across keys.

## 🔁 Retry

`POST /items/{id}/retry` re-drives a failed item in place rather than re-enqueuing the URL. It refuses anything but a `failed` item, and a `failed` item past the retry cap, with `409`; `404` for an unknown id. An accepted retry sets the item back to `queued`, rewrites `queued_at`, advances `retry_count`, clears the old error, and hands the item to the queued lifecycle task, the same task enqueue uses.

What the task does depends on how far the previous run got: [item-lifecycle](item-lifecycle.md) carries each case and what it costs.

> [!NOTE] Double-submitting is refused by the write, not by the read
> The transition is one conditional `UPDATE` gating on status still `failed` and `retry_count` under the cap, incrementing the count in SQL. A rowcount of zero is the `409`. Reading the row first and then writing would let two concurrent retries both pass the guard, which costs two Modal spawns for one item and increments the count once, so the cap would read tighter than it is. The pre-read only picks which refusal message to send.

> [!NOTE] Why the cap is local and quota is not
> The per-item retry cap (`retry_max`, default 3) is a cheap local bound on the worst case: a flapping item spends at most a few synthesises before it stays failed. Broader per-key and quota enforcement is deliberately not built here. The cap does not need the full hardening apparatus, and building half of one here would be worse than either.

## ⏩ What is not built yet

- **Quota and API-key management.** No enforcement and no create/revoke route exist yet.
- **A list endpoint.** There is no `GET /items` today; a client tracks ids itself.
- **Word-level timing.** One window per unit, not per word, by design; see [read-along-timing](read-along-timing.md).
